name: Deliver a sustaining capital project
summary: Project managers in the engineering division deliver approved sustaining capital projects (equipment replacements, controls upgrades, protection and electrical work, environmental and safety improvements) from scope through design, approvals, procurement, construction and commissioning to handover. They work with engineering consultants, electrical and plant engineers, supply chain, contractors, safety advisors and plant operations. Projects are slow because design, long-lead equipment and regulatory approvals take months, and many must wait for a planned outage before work can start; scope gaps and late as-built documents cause change orders and delayed closeouts.

baseline.org_archetype: An Alberta merchant generator with about 1,300 staff, three gas steam units converted from coal at the Wabamun-area sites, two cogeneration plants, 17 hydro plants and 12 wind farms, with a central engineering and asset management division of about 130 people.
baseline.notes: Reference period 2019 to 2022. Large coal-to-gas conversions were run by the energy transition division and are not in this file's volume.

trigger: The annual budget approves the project line.
end_state: The project is commissioned, handed over to operations, capitalised and closed, or it is cancelled at the funding gate.

volume.seasonality: Most projects open in the first quarter after budget approval; construction peaks in summer and in outage seasons.

evidence.note: Whole-company sustaining capital was 141 to 218 million CAD a year in 2017-2019 and 150 to 170 million was planned for 2022 (tac2019mda, tac2021ir), much of it planned major maintenance and routine capital. About 40 to 60 projects a year of 0.5 to 3 million CAD each is the author's estimate; with 12 to 18 month durations this gives the 40 to 80 active projects in the organisation file.
14 project managers; the rest of their time goes to capital planning estimates and conversion support.
Electrical and protection design reviews.
Operability reviews and commissioning; not listed in the organisation file's roles for this process.
Contractor safety plans and hazard assessments; not listed in the organisation file's roles for this process.
Turnover packages and drawing updates.
Capitalisation; not listed in the organisation file's roles for this process.
Funding gate approvals; not listed in the organisation file's roles for this process.

systems.name: ERP (finance, purchasing and plant maintenance modules)
Document management and engineering drawings repository
Outage and project scheduling software (critical path)
AER and Alberta Environment submission portals

steps.name: Receive approved budget and open the project
steps.description: When the annual budget is approved, the project manager receives the project line (asset, purpose, budget, target year), opens a project and cost collector in the ERP, and sets up the project folder and register in the document store.

evidence.note: Projects start after the annual budget approval; queue time until a project manager is free is estimated.

steps.name: Define scope and basis of design
steps.description: The project manager meets the plant, hydro or wind site and the reliability engineer, visits the asset, and writes the scope, basis of design, constraints (outage window, permits, tie-ins) and success criteria in a project charter.

error.defect_description: Scope misses a tie-in or an operating constraint, found in design review or construction.

evidence.note: Scope definition by the project manager with operations is common practice; hours estimated.

steps.name: Estimate cost and schedule
steps.description: The project manager builds a cost estimate from vendor budget quotes and past projects and a schedule in the scheduling tool, including long-lead equipment and the outage window if the work needs the unit offline.

error.defect_description: Estimate too low; leads to change orders and a budget variance.

evidence.note: Common practice; hours estimated.

steps.name: Pass the execution funding gate
steps.description: The vice-president of engineering reviews scope, estimate, schedule and risks at the gate review and releases execution funding under the delegation of authority, sends the project back for rework or cancels it.

control.basis: Corporate delegation of financial authority and capital project stage-gate procedure

evidence.note: Stage-gate funding release under delegation of authority is common practice; shares estimated.

steps.name: Wait for detailed design from engineering consultant
steps.description: An engineering consultant on a standing agreement prepares drawings, specifications and calculations, which are stamped by a professional engineer, while the project manager answers questions.

control.basis: Alberta Engineering and Geoscience Professions Act: authentication of engineering documents by a professional engineer

evidence.note: Detailed design durations of one to five months estimated.

steps.name: Review electrical and protection design
steps.description: The electrical and protection engineer checks single-line diagrams, protection settings, cable sizing and grid connection requirements against company standards and AESO and transmission requirements, and marks up comments.

evidence.note: Common practice; hours estimated.

steps.name: Review design for operability
steps.description: The plant engineer and operations representatives review the design for operability, maintainability and safety (a hazard review for process changes) and return comments; the consultant issues the design for construction.

error.defect_description: Operability problem missed; found at commissioning.

control.basis: Company management of change and process hazard review standard

evidence.note: Hazard and operability review for process changes is common practice; the share needing a new regulatory approval is estimated.

steps.name: Prepare regulatory filing request
steps.description: Where the project changes a power plant approval, an environmental approval or a pressure equipment design, the project manager prepares the technical content and sends a filing request to the regulatory team, which files with the AUC, the AER or Alberta Environment, or registers the design with ABSA.

control.basis: AUC Rule 007 power plant applications; Alberta Pressure Equipment Safety Regulation design registration

evidence.note: Power plant alterations can need AUC approval and pressure piping designs need ABSA registration; the process is described from general knowledge.

steps.name: Wait for regulatory approval
steps.description: The AUC, the AER, Alberta Environment or ABSA reviews the application or design registration, may send information requests that the regulatory team answers with the project manager, and returns an approval with conditions.

evidence.note: Approval times of one to six months estimated.

steps.name: Raise material requests for equipment
steps.description: The project manager raises material requests in the ERP for the equipment and bulk materials named in the design, with specifications, technical evaluation criteria and required-on-site dates, for supply chain to tender and order.

error.defect_description: Specification error on a material request.

evidence.note: Common practice; hours estimated.

steps.name: Prepare construction scope and evaluate contractor bids
steps.description: The project manager writes the construction scope of work and, after supply chain tenders it, evaluates contractor bids for price, schedule, safety record and qualifications and recommends an award.

evidence.note: Common practice; hours estimated.

steps.name: Wait for equipment delivery
steps.description: The project waits for vendors to fabricate and deliver equipment; the project manager reviews vendor drawings and progress reports, and long-lead items such as transformers, breakers and large valves can take six months or more.

evidence.note: Equipment lead times of six weeks to nine months estimated; the share of projects that need an outage is the author's estimate based on the organisation file's statement that many projects are finished inside planned outages.

steps.name: Wait for the planned outage window
steps.description: Work that needs the unit offline waits for the next planned outage. The project manager gives the outage planners the scope, durations and tie-in points so the work is put in the outage schedule.

evidence.note: Outages for converted units are generally annual, so projects wait up to a year for a window.

steps.name: Raise the engineering change
steps.description: The project manager raises the engineering change (management of change) record with the design, risk review and operating changes, so drawings, procedures and training are updated before the change is put into service.

evidence.note: The organisation file links capital projects to the engineering change process.

steps.name: Review contractor safety plan and run pre-job hazard assessment
steps.description: The safety advisor reviews the contractor's site-specific safety plan, confirms orientation and tickets, and attends the pre-job hazard assessment for high-risk tasks such as lifts, excavation, energised work and hot work.

control.basis: Alberta OHS Code Part 2 hazard assessment; company contractor safety standard

evidence.note: Hazard assessment before work is required under the Alberta OHS Code; safety advisors are shared across sites.

steps.name: Install and construct
steps.description: The contractor installs the equipment and makes the tie-ins under permits: civil works, mechanical installation, cabling and terminations, using the mobile crane for heavy lifts. Outdoor work stops for high winds and extreme cold.

evidence.note: Installation durations of two weeks to several months estimated (touch is elapsed working time of the contractor crew, not person-hours); Alberta winter conditions stop outdoor work on some days.

steps.name: Travel to site for supervision
steps.description: The project manager drives to the site for weekly construction meetings and inspections during installation. The time here is the total over the construction period.

evidence.note: Weekly site visits from the engineering office estimated.

steps.name: Supervise construction and approve change orders
steps.description: On site and by email the project manager checks progress and quality against the design, resolves field problems with the consultant, and reviews and approves contractor change orders within the project contingency.

error.defect_description: Change order approved above its value or without scope check.

evidence.note: Hours estimated.

steps.name: Report monthly cost and progress
steps.description: Each month the project manager updates the cost forecast from ERP commitments and accruals, the schedule and the risk list, and sends the project report to the engineering vice-president and finance. The time here is the total over the project.

evidence.note: Monthly project reporting is common practice; this is the unit of work the organisation file uses for this process.

steps.name: Commission and test with operations
steps.description: The plant engineer leads pre-commissioning checks and functional tests with the contractor and operators, works through the punch list and confirms the equipment meets the design before operations accepts it.

evidence.note: Commissioning with operations is common practice; failure share estimated.

steps.name: Hand over drawings and turnover package
steps.description: The document controller collects as-built drawings, vendor manuals, test records and the updated engineering change from the consultant and contractor, checks them against the turnover checklist, chases missing items and files them in the drawings repository.

evidence.note: Document turnover is common practice; as-builts are often late.

steps.name: Settle project costs to fixed assets
steps.description: An accountant settles the project cost collector to fixed asset records, splits costs between new assets and retirements and records the in-service date for depreciation.

control.basis: IFRS property, plant and equipment capitalisation and internal control over financial reporting

evidence.note: Capitalisation at month end is common practice.

steps.name: Write closeout report and lessons learned
steps.description: The project manager compares final cost and schedule with the approved estimate, explains variances, records lessons learned and closes the project in the ERP.

evidence.note: Common practice; closeouts are often delayed by late invoices.

exceptions.name: Regulatory approval needed
exceptions.description: The project changes a power plant, environmental or pressure equipment approval, and work waits for the regulator.

exceptions.name: Waiting for an outage window
exceptions.description: Tie-ins need the unit offline, so construction waits for the next planned outage, often months after the equipment arrives.

exceptions.name: Failed commissioning
exceptions.description: A functional test fails and the contractor returns to fix the installation.

exceptions.name: Scope or estimate sent back at the gate
exceptions.description: The funding gate returns the project for more scope definition or a better estimate.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from budget approval to project closeout
benchmarks.population: Sustaining capital projects at an Alberta generator, 2019-2022

evidence.note: Author's estimate: design, procurement and an outage window put most sustaining projects at 12 to 18 months, with large or regulated projects near two years.

benchmarks.unit: million CAD per year, whole company

evidence.note: Includes planned major maintenance and mine capital, not only projects run by project managers.

pain_points.description: Long-lead equipment and the wait for an outage window set the schedule more than the work itself.

evidence.note: Author's estimate; the organisation file notes many projects must finish inside a planned outage.

pain_points.description: Scope gaps from early definition show up as change orders during construction.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

pain_points.description: As-built drawings and vendor documents arrive late, so turnover and closeout drag on after the equipment is in service.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

pain_points.description: Monthly cost reports are assembled by hand from ERP commitments and spreadsheets.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of 2019-2022 practice.

assumptions: The unit of work is one project from budget approval to closeout. The organisation file counts active project-months (40 to 80); 3 to 6 project starts a month with 12 to 18 month durations gives the same number of active projects.

Project manager work spread over months (site visits, construction supervision, monthly reports) is recorded once per project as total hours in s17 to s19 with near-zero waits; those steps run alongside construction.
Contractor and consultant work uses the role external and is not costed in labour.
Regulatory approvals are filed by hse-regulatory-filings; this file counts only the project manager's input and the wait.
Loaded costs are taken from the organisation file (wage x 1.40).

The simulated median (about 490 days) is about 1.2 times the 420-day benchmark because design, equipment fabrication and the contractor tender run one after another in the step graph, while in practice the tender and some procurement overlap with design.
The FTE implied by touch time (about 21) includes about 150 hours per project of contractor and consultant time on external steps; without it the implied internal FTE is close to the 14.5 stated.
